messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kaito's life was forever changed on a fateful day in August when a category 5 typhoon tore through his coastal hometown. The howling winds and relentless rain had seemed to last an eternity as he huddled with his family in their small apartment. The sounds of shattering glass, crumbling walls, and screams still echoed in his mind like they were yesterday. As the storm raged on, Kaito's neck was wrenched in a sudden gust, leaving him with a chronic ache that flared up without warning. It was these moments of pain that would often transport Kaito back to that day. The memory felt almost surreal – as if it had happened to someone else. He couldn't shake the feeling that he'd simply imagined the entire ordeal, that it was all just some macabre fantasy born from his own fevered imagination. And yet, every time the memory resurfaced, the taste of saltwater and mud flooded his senses, leaving him gasping for air. As Kaito struggled to reconcile the past with his present life in the city, he found himself increasingly withdrawn. His work as a UX designer was suffering – not because he couldn't focus, but because he felt like an outsider, looking in on the world through a distorted lens. People seemed fake, their smiles and laughter just thin veneers hiding darker intentions. He felt disconnected from his colleagues, his friends, even himself. Feeling physically unwell also became a regular occurrence – usually after a long night of working late or socializing with others. It was as if his body had become attuned to the slightest hint of stress, responding by making him feel queasy and lightheaded. Kaito began to avoid social gatherings, fearing that one wrong move would set off another panic attack. He couldn't explain why these small triggers – a neck pain here, a feeling of illness there – seemed to have such an outsize impact on his life. It was as if every event, no matter how minor, threatened to spiral him back into the heart of that storm. This feeling of being constantly on edge only served to further entrench Kaito's negative appraisals: people were not trustworthy; he didn't belong anywhere. Kaito started noticing how certain events – anniversaries of the typhoon, or news reports about natural disasters – would send him tumbling down a rabbit hole of memories and emotions. The anniversary was particularly fraught, as it coincided with a major design project deadline at work. Feeling overwhelmed by both past traumas and present responsibilities, Kaito lashed out at his colleagues during an important meeting. That incident marked the final straw – Kaito realized that he needed help to break this cycle of pain, memories, and isolation. As he sat in his dark apartment, nursing a wounded pride and a sore neck, Kaito knew it was time to confront the storm within him head-on.
